title: Part 2, Chapter 14
paragraphs: In which the adventure of the Knight of the Grove continues

Among the things that passed between Don Quixote and the Knight of the Wood, the history records that the Knight of the Grove said to Don Quixote, “The truth is, sir knight, that my destiny — or, to speak more accurately, my own choice — led me to fall in love with the peerless Casildea de Vandalia. I call her peerless because she has no equal, whether in bodily stature or in supremacy of rank and beauty. This Casildea I speak of repaid my honorable passion and courteous devotion the way Hercules’s stepmother repaid him: by driving me into one danger after another, promising at the end of each that when the next was finished, the object of my hopes would finally be granted. But my labors have multiplied, link upon link, until they are past counting, and I no longer know which will be the last one that marks the beginning of the fulfillment of my chaste desires. Once she sent me to challenge the famous giantess of Seville, La Giralda by name, who is as mighty and powerful as if she were cast in brass, and who, though she never stirs from one spot, is the most restless and fickle woman in the world. I came, I saw, I conquered, and I made her stand still and behave herself, for nothing but north winds blew for more than a week. Another time she ordered me to lift those ancient stones, the mighty bulls of Guisando — a task more fit for porters than for knights. On yet another occasion she commanded me to hurl myself into the cavern of Cabra — an unequaled and terrifying peril — and bring her a detailed account of everything hidden in those gloomy depths. I stopped the Giralda’s turning, I lifted the bulls of Guisando, I threw myself into the cavern and brought the secrets of its abyss up into the light; and still my hopes are as dead as dead can be, while her scorn and her commands are as alive as ever. To make a long story short, she has lately ordered me to travel through every province of Spain and force every knight-errant wandering there to confess that she surpasses all women alive today in beauty, and that I am the bravest and most deeply enamored knight on earth. In pursuit of this claim I have already crossed the greater part of Spain and defeated a number of knights who dared to contradict me; but what I plume and pride myself on most is having beaten in single combat that famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, and having made him confess that my Casildea is more beautiful than his Dulcinea. With that one victory I count myself the conqueror of every knight in the world, for this Don Quixote I speak of has defeated them all, and since I have defeated him, his glory, his fame, and his honor have passed over and been transferred to my person; for

The greater the renown the vanquished bears,
the greater is the glory the victor wears.
And so the countless exploits of this Don Quixote I have named are now set down to my account and have become my own.”

Don Quixote was astonished to hear the Knight of the Grove, and a thousand times he was on the point of telling him he lied; the flat denial was already on the tip of his tongue. But he restrained himself as best he could, so as to make the knight confess the lie out of his own mouth, and so he said to him calmly, “As for your claim, sir knight, to have defeated most of the knights of Spain, or even of the whole world, I say nothing; but that you have defeated Don Quixote of La Mancha I take leave to doubt. It may have been someone else who resembled him, though there are few who do.”

“What! Not defeated?” said the Knight of the Grove. “By the heaven above us, I fought Don Quixote and beat him and made him surrender. He is a tall man with a gaunt face and long, lanky limbs, his hair going gray, his nose aquiline and rather hooked, and his mustache black, large, and drooping. He fights under the name of ‘The Countenance,’ and he has for a squire a peasant named Sancho Panza; he presses the flanks and guides the reins of a famous steed called Rocinante; and finally, the mistress of his heart is a certain Dulcinea del Toboso, once upon a time known as Aldonza Lorenzo — just as I call mine Casildea de Vandalia, because her name is Casilda and she comes from Andalusia. If all these signs are not enough to prove the truth of what I say, here is my sword, which will force disbelief itself to believe it.”

“Calm yourself, sir knight,” said Don Quixote, “and listen to what I am about to tell you. You should know that this Don Quixote you speak of is the greatest friend I have in this world — so much so that I might say I regard him as I do my own person — and from the precise and unmistakable description you have given, I cannot help thinking he must be the very man you defeated. On the other hand, I see with my own eyes and feel with my own hands that it cannot possibly have been the same man; unless, since he has many enemies who are enchanters — one in particular who persecutes him constantly — one of them took on his shape and allowed himself to be beaten, in order to cheat him of the fame that his lofty deeds of chivalry have earned and won for him throughout the known world. And to confirm this, I must tell you something more: barely ten hours ago those same enchanters, his enemies, transformed the figure and person of the fair Dulcinea del Toboso into a coarse, lowly village girl, and in the same way they must have transformed Don Quixote. And if all this is not enough to persuade you of the truth of what I say, here stands Don Quixote himself, who will uphold it with arms, on foot or on horseback or in whatever manner you please.”

And as he said this he rose to his feet and gripped his sword, waiting to see what the Knight of the Grove would do. The other answered in an equally calm voice, “A good payer is not troubled by giving a pledge. The man who managed to defeat you once when you were transformed, Sir Don Quixote, may reasonably hope to overcome you in your own true shape. But since it is not fitting for knights to perform their feats of arms in the dark, like highwaymen and ruffians, let us wait for daylight, so that the sun may witness our deeds. And the conditions of our combat shall be these: the loser shall place himself at the winner’s disposal, to do whatever he commands, provided his commands are such as befit a knight.”

“I am more than satisfied with these terms and conditions,” Don Quixote replied; and with that they went over to where their squires lay and found them snoring, in the very same posture in which sleep had overtaken them. They woke them and ordered them to make the horses ready, since at sunrise the two of them were to meet in a bloody, hard-fought single combat. At this news Sancho was stunned and thunderstruck, trembling for his master’s safety because of the mighty deeds he had heard the squire of the Grove attribute to his own; but without a word the two squires went off in search of their animals, for by now the three horses and the ass had sniffed one another out and were all standing together.

On the way, the squire of the Grove said to Sancho, “You should know, brother, that among the fighting men of Andalusia it is the custom, when they stand as godfathers in any quarrel, not to wait idly with folded arms while their godsons fight. I mention this to remind you that while our masters are fighting, we have to fight too, and smash each other to splinters.”

“That custom, sir squire,” Sancho replied, “may pass among the ruffians and fighting men you mention, but among the squires of knights-errant, certainly not. At least, I have never heard my master mention any such custom, and he knows all the laws of knight-errantry by heart. But even granting it’s true that there is an express law requiring squires to fight while their masters fight, I don’t intend to obey it; I would rather pay whatever penalty is laid on peaceable squires like myself, for I am sure it cannot come to more than two pounds of wax, and I would sooner pay that, since I know it will cost me less than the lint I shall have to buy to bandage my head — which I already count as broken and split in two. And there is another thing that makes fighting impossible for me: I have no sword, for I have never carried one in my life.”
“I know a good cure for that,” said the squire of the Grove. “I have here two linen bags of the same size; you shall take one and I the other, and we will fight with bag blows, on equal terms.”
“If that’s how it is, then with all my heart,” said Sancho, “for a battle of that kind will do more to knock the dust out of us than to hurt us.”

“That won’t do,” said the other, “because to keep the wind from carrying them off we must put into the bags half a dozen nice smooth pebbles, all of the same weight; and that way we can thump one another without doing ourselves any harm or damage.”

“By my father’s body!” said Sancho. “Look at the marten and sable and pads of carded cotton he’s stuffing into the bags, so that our heads won’t be cracked and our bones won’t be pounded to jelly! But even if they were filled with silk floss, I can tell you, señor, I am not going to fight. Let our masters fight — that’s their business — and let us drink and live; for time will take care of relieving us of our lives without our going out hunting for blows to finish them off before their proper season, when they will drop from sheer ripeness.”
“Even so,” replied the squire of the Grove, “we have to fight, if only for half an hour.”

“Absolutely not,” said Sancho. “I am not going to be so rude or so ungrateful as to pick a quarrel, however small, with a man I have eaten and drunk with. Besides, who the devil could bring himself to fight stone cold, without anger and without provocation?”

“I can fix that completely,” said the squire of the Grove, “and here is how: before we begin the battle, I will walk up to your worship nice and gently and give you three or four punches that will stretch you out at my feet and wake up your anger, even if it’s sleeping sounder than a dormouse.”

“To match that plan,” said Sancho, “I have another that doesn’t fall a hair behind it: I will take a cudgel, and before your worship gets close enough to wake my anger, I will put yours so soundly to sleep with whacks that it won’t wake again except in the next world — where it is well known that I am not a man to let anyone lay a hand on my face. Let every man watch out for the arrow; though the safer course would be to let everyone’s anger go on sleeping, for nobody knows another man’s heart, and a fellow can go out for wool and come home shorn. God gave his blessing to peace and his curse to quarrels; and if a hunted cat, cornered and hard pressed, turns into a lion, God knows what I, who am a man, might turn into. So from this moment on I give you notice, sir squire, that all the harm and damage that comes of our quarrel will be charged to your account.”
“Very well,” said the squire of the Grove. “God will send the dawn, and we shall manage somehow.”

And now bright-feathered birds of every kind began to sing in the trees, and with their varied, joyful notes they seemed to greet and welcome the fresh morning, who was already showing the beauty of her face at the gates and balconies of the east, shaking from her hair a shower of liquid pearls. Bathed in that sweet moisture, the plants too seemed to scatter and rain down a spray of tiny pearls; the willows dripped delicious manna, the fountains laughed, the brooks murmured, the woods rejoiced, and the meadows dressed themselves in all their finery at her coming. But scarcely had the light of day made it possible to see and tell one thing from another when the first object that met Sancho Panza’s eyes was the nose of the squire of the Grove, so big that it almost cast a shadow over his whole body. It is recorded, in fact, that it was of enormous size, hooked in the middle, covered with warts, and mulberry-colored, like an eggplant; it hung a good two fingers’ length below his mouth, and its size, its color, its warts, and its crook made his face so hideous that Sancho, looking at him, began to shake hand and foot like a child in convulsions, and he vowed in his heart to take two hundred punches sooner than let his anger be provoked into fighting that monster. Don Quixote examined his opponent and found that he already had his helmet on with the visor lowered, so that his face could not be seen; he noticed, however, that he was a solidly built man, though not very tall. Over his armor he wore a surcoat or cassock of what looked like the finest cloth of gold, spangled all over with glittering mirrors like little moons, which gave him a remarkably gallant and showy appearance; above his helmet waved a great mass of plumes — green, yellow, and white — and his lance, propped against a tree, was very long and thick, with a steel point more than a palm in length.

Don Quixote observed it all and took note of it all, and from what he saw and noted he concluded that this knight must be a man of great strength; but for all that he did not give way to fear, as Sancho Panza had. Instead, with a composed and fearless air, he said to the Knight of the Mirrors, “If your great eagerness to fight, sir knight, has not used up your courtesy, then in courtesy’s name I ask you to raise your visor a little, so that I may see whether the handsomeness of your face matches that of your equipment.”

“Whether you come out of this enterprise victorious or defeated, sir knight,” replied the Knight of the Mirrors, “you will have more than enough time and leisure to look at me; and if I do not grant your request now, it is because it seems to me I would do a serious wrong to the fair Casildea de Vandalia by wasting the time it would take to raise my visor before forcing you to confess what you already know I maintain.”
“Well then,” said Don Quixote, “while we mount our horses you can at least tell me whether I am the Don Quixote you claim to have defeated.”

“To that we answer,” said the Knight of the Mirrors, “that you resemble the very knight I defeated as closely as one egg resembles another; but since you say that enchanters persecute you, I will not venture to state positively whether you are that man or not.”

“That,” said Don Quixote, “is enough to convince me that you are laboring under a deception; nevertheless, to free you from it entirely, let our horses be brought, and in less time than it would take you to raise your visor — if God, my lady, and my arm stand by me — I shall see your face, and you shall see that I am not the defeated Don Quixote you take me for.”

With that, cutting the conversation short, they mounted, and Don Quixote wheeled Rocinante around to take the proper distance for charging back at his opponent, and the Knight of the Mirrors did the same; but Don Quixote had not gone twenty paces when he heard the other calling him, and when each had come back halfway, the Knight of the Mirrors said to him, “Remember, sir knight, that the terms of our combat are that the loser, as I said before, shall be at the winner’s disposal.”
“I am already aware of it,” said Don Quixote, “provided that whatever is commanded and imposed on the loser does not go beyond the limits of chivalry.”
“That is understood,” replied the Knight of the Mirrors.

At that moment the squire’s extraordinary nose presented itself to Don Quixote’s view, and he was no less astonished at the sight than Sancho had been — so much so that he set the man down as some kind of monster, or a human being of some new species or unearthly breed. Sancho, seeing his master ride off to take his run, had no wish to be left alone with the nose-man, fearing that one flick of that nose against his own would end the whole battle for him, and he would be left stretched on the ground either from the blow or from sheer fright; so he ran after his master, clinging to one of Rocinante’s stirrup-straps, and when it seemed to him time for Don Quixote to turn, he said, “I beg your worship, señor, before you wheel around to charge, help me climb up into this cork tree, where I will be able to watch the gallant encounter your worship is going to have with this knight better, and more to my liking, than from the ground.”
“It seems to me, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “that what you really want is a grandstand seat, so you can watch the bulls without any danger.”
“To tell the truth,” Sancho answered, “that squire’s monstrous nose has filled me with such fear and terror that I don’t dare stay anywhere near him.”
“It is indeed,” said Don Quixote, “the kind of nose that would frighten me too, if I were not who I am; so come along, and I will help you up wherever you like.”

While Don Quixote paused to help Sancho up into the cork tree, the Knight of the Mirrors took as much ground as he thought he needed, and, assuming Don Quixote had done the same, without waiting for a trumpet blast or any other signal to set them off, he wheeled his horse — which was no more agile or better-looking than Rocinante — and at his top speed, which was an easy trot, set out to charge his enemy. Seeing him busy getting Sancho up the tree, however, he pulled on the reins and stopped halfway through his run, for which his horse was deeply grateful, being unable to go a step further. Don Quixote, imagining that his enemy was bearing down on him at full flight, dug his spurs hard into Rocinante’s bony flanks and made him stretch out in such style that, the history tells us, this was the only occasion on which he was known to manage something like a gallop — on every other it was plain trotting with him — and with this unheard-of fury he bore down on the Knight of the Mirrors, who sat digging his spurs into his horse up to the buttons without being able to move him a finger’s length from the spot where his run had come to a dead stop. At this lucky moment and crisis, Don Quixote came upon his adversary, struggling with his horse and tangled up with his lance, which he either could not manage or had no time to set in its rest. Don Quixote, paying no attention to these difficulties, and in complete safety and without the slightest risk to himself, struck the Knight of the Mirrors with such force that he sent him to the ground over his horse’s haunches in spite of himself, with a fall so heavy that he lay there to all appearances dead, not moving hand or foot. The instant Sancho saw him fall, he slid down from the cork tree and hurried over to his master, who, dismounting from Rocinante, went and stood over the Knight of the Mirrors, and unlacing his helmet to see whether he was dead — and to give him air if he happened to be alive — he saw... who can say what he saw, without filling everyone who hears it with astonishment, wonder, and awe? He saw, the history says, the very countenance, the very face, the very look, the very features, the very form, the very image of the bachelor Samson Carrasco! And the moment he saw it he shouted, “Come quickly, Sancho, and look at what you are going to see and not believe! Hurry, my son, and learn what magic can do, and what wizards and enchanters are capable of.”

Sancho came over, and when he saw the bachelor Carrasco’s face he began crossing himself a thousand times and blessing himself a thousand more. All this while the fallen knight showed no sign of life, and Sancho said to Don Quixote, “In my opinion, señor, just to be safe, your worship should take your sword and thrust it into the mouth of this fellow here who looks like the bachelor Samson Carrasco; maybe in him you will kill one of those enemies of yours, the enchanters.”

“Your advice is not bad,” said Don Quixote, “for where enemies are concerned, the fewer the better;” and he was drawing his sword to carry out Sancho’s counsel and suggestion when the squire of the Mirrors came running up, now without the nose that had made him so hideous, and shouted, “Watch what you are doing, Señor Don Quixote! The man lying at your feet is your friend, the bachelor Samson Carrasco, and I am his squire.”

“And the nose?” said Sancho, seeing him without the hideous feature he had worn before; to which he answered, “I have it here in my pocket,” and reaching into his right pocket he pulled out a masquerade nose of varnished pasteboard, of the make already described; and Sancho, studying him more and more closely, cried out in a voice of amazement, “Holy Mary be good to me! Isn’t it Tom Cecial, my neighbor and old crony?”

“Of course I am!” replied the now noseless squire. “Tom Cecial I am, crony and friend of Sancho Panza, and in a moment I will tell you all the schemes and tricks and lies that brought me here; but in the meantime, beg and plead with your master not to touch, mistreat, wound, or kill the Knight of the Mirrors lying at his feet, because beyond any dispute he is the rash and badly advised bachelor Samson Carrasco, our fellow townsman.”

At that moment the Knight of the Mirrors came to his senses, and Don Quixote, seeing it, held the bare point of his sword over his face and said to him, “You are a dead man, knight, unless you confess that the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso surpasses your Casildea de Vandalia in beauty. And beyond this you must promise — if you should survive this encounter and this fall — to go to the city of El Toboso and present yourself before her on my behalf, so that she may deal with you as she pleases; and if she leaves you free to do as you please, you are likewise to return and seek me out — the trail of my mighty deeds will serve as a guide to bring you wherever I may be — and tell me what passed between you and her. These conditions, in keeping with what we agreed before our combat, do not overstep the proper bounds of knight-errantry.”

“I confess,” said the fallen knight, “that the dirty, tattered shoe of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso is worth more than the unkempt though clean beard of Casildea, and I promise to go to her presence and return from it to yours, and to give you a full and detailed account of everything you ask of me.”

“You must also confess and believe,” Don Quixote added, “that the knight you defeated was not and could not have been Don Quixote of La Mancha, but someone else who looked like him — just as I confess and believe that you, though you appear to be the bachelor Samson Carrasco, are not he, but someone else in his likeness, whom my enemies have set before me in his shape so that I may check and temper the force of my anger and make gentle use of the glory of my victory.”

“I confess, hold, and believe everything just as you believe, hold, and think it,” said the battered knight. “Let me get up, I beg you — if, that is, the shock of my fall allows it, for it has left me in a sorry enough state.”

Don Quixote helped him to his feet, with the assistance of his squire Tom Cecial, from whom Sancho never took his eyes, asking him question after question; and the answers he received gave clear proof that the man really and truly was the Tom Cecial he claimed to be. Yet the impression his master’s words had stamped on Sancho’s mind — that the enchanters had changed the face of the Knight of the Mirrors into that of the bachelor Samson Carrasco — would not let him believe what his own eyes were seeing. In the end, both master and servant remained in their delusion; and the Knight of the Mirrors and his squire, crestfallen and down on their luck, parted from Don Quixote and Sancho, the knight intending to find some village where he could plaster and bandage his ribs. Don Quixote and Sancho went on with their journey to Saragossa, and there the history leaves them, so that it may relate who the Knight of the Mirrors and his long-nosed squire really were.
